accuracy.evidence: Rules checked word for word against English Appendix 1 (National Curriculum in England), Years 5–6: '-fer' r doubled if still stressed (referring, referred, referral, preferring, preferred, transferring, transferred) and single if not (reference, referee, preference, transference); 'i before e except after c' applies to /iː/ (deceive, conceive, receive, perceive, ceiling; exceptions protein, caffeine, seize); ough list (ought, bought, thought, rough, tough, enough, cough, though, dough, through, plough, bough). Stress patterns of every lab word checked in the Cambridge and Oxford Learner's dictionaries (re-FER, REF-er-ence, re-FER-ral, PREF-er-ence, con-FER-ring, ref-er-EE, IN-fer-ence, CON-fer-ence). Letter counts in p6/p7 enumerated: refer 5→referring 9, prefer 6→preferred 9.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: doubling every -fer word (preferrence, referree) or none (prefered, referal); over-applying ei after c to non-/iː/ words (sceince, anceint); and assuming ough words that look alike rhyme (though/through). Each wrong tap names the stressed syllable or the sound that decides it.

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab's mechanism is this topic's: a tappable syllable strip whose stressed beat lights up, -fer + suffix builds where the strip explains the doubling, ie/ei gap fills including the science exception, a six-sound ough sorter and a proofreading note mixing all three rules. It shares no mechanic with flagable (-able/-ible), flaghyph (prefix hyphens) or the word-list lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners first discover that stress moves (refer vs reference) by tapping beats, then use that to predict doubling; the lab shows the stressed syllable after each build so the rule is seen, not told. The ough sort makes them hear six sounds for one string before the text names it.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions with tempting wrong options: FER for reference, preferrence, recieve, and 'Yes, they look alike' for though/through; each is disproved by the task that follows and A.reveal states the result.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge items with tagged wrong options (fer1, fer2, drop, cei, soft, sh, eesound, rhyme, front), each with a specific correction such as 'Say trans-FER-red. The stress stays on -fer, so double the r.'

readability.evidence: Kid explanation FK grade 0.5 and adult 9.1 (limits 6.5 and 9.5) by learn/readability.py; stress is defined before it is used, and every rule comes with two example words.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph is one rule with examples, or the lab plan, or the named mistakes; no filler phrases; the content gate's 12% similarity check against all lessons passes.

mobile.evidence: Large syllable tiles (min 64 px wide, 66 px tall), two big choice tiles for spellings and ie/ei, the ough grid drops to 2 columns under 520 px, and the proofreading note wraps word by word; every action also has a button. Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots.

accessibility.evidence: All taps and drags have buttons (Loud beat: …, both spellings, ie/ei, sound buttons, Check “word”); the canvas aria-label carries the current word, choices and progress; axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in light and dark themes on desktop and phone (walk.cjs).

sources: Department for Education (2013), The national curriculum in England: English programmes of study, English Appendix 1: Spelling, Years 5 and 6
